solution: The 'Nepal' paragraph describes exactly an open (free) border: "The foundation of friendship between India and Nepal was laid with Indo-Nepalese Friendship Treaty in 1950. According to this treaty, Nepalese citizens can not only enter India, but they are also permitted to take up government jobs and carry on trade in India." Pakistan is described only through Kashmir, infiltration and the Sir Creek dispute; Bangladesh through border and river treaties; Myanmar as a 'door' being opened by new rail and road links — none of them free-movement borders. (The chapter never uses the phrase 'free international border' itself, so the match rests on the treaty description.)

The chapter gives Pakistan and China their own conflict sections — Indo-Pak relations turn on world-view differences, Kashmir and nuclear rivalry with dialogue "proving to be unsuccessful", and "there are tensions in Sino-Indian relations" over the border and Tibet. Every other option is described as friendly: Nepal and Bhutan (treaty friendship, India bearing Bhutan's defence), Myanmar and Maldives (trade and cooperation), Afghanistan and America (Indian aid; Indo-US relations "completely transformed").

The chapter enumerates precisely these three: "Indo-Pak relations are influenced by three main factors : (1) Differences in the world views of both the countries (2) the Kashmir question and (3) Nuclear rivalry between the two countries." Since all three named options are on the chapter's own list, no single one can be the answer and 'All of the above' is forced.
